I am less interested in being told that a building is modern because more of it was made in a factory.

The customer is buying a completed building. They need to know what it will cost, when it will be ready, how it will perform and who will stand behind it. If an off-site method gives them a demonstrably better deal, it deserves serious consideration. That is where the conversation should begin.

Too often we begin with the method and work backwards towards a reason to use it.

Subscribe now

What problem are we solving?

Prefab is a broad label. It can describe a component, a panel, a serviced assembly or a complete room. These involve different design decisions, commercial arrangements and site operations. Treating them as one product obscures the choices that matter.

A useful proposal identifies the problem first. Perhaps it is difficult access, repeated work at height, an unreliable sequence of trades, or a programme exposed to too much weather. Perhaps a repeatable assembly can improve dimensional control and reduce rework. Explain that problem, then show how the proposed method deals with it.

Moving fabrication into a more controlled environment can be valuable. It can also move costs and risks into places the client has not previously had to consider. Transport, storage, lifting, connections, inspections and the timing of payments all belong in the assessment. A factory price is not the cost of an installed, functioning part of a building.

The same discipline should apply to the conventional alternative. Established practice should not win by default simply because its inefficiencies are familiar.

The project has to be ready for the product

In a 2014 article, I questioned claims about the benefits of off-site construction after observing a London project in late 2012. My concern was with the organisation of the work: lifting sequences, interruptions and exposure to weather. Components arriving from a factory did not, by themselves, settle those questions.

That was one observation at one point in a project. It was not a controlled comparison of two construction methods. Its value was the question it raised: how much of a component’s potential advantage survives the way the project is actually run?

That question is still worth asking.

A manufactured assembly needs a coordinated place to go. Its dimensions, connections and service interfaces must be resolved. The access and lifting plan must work. The installation team needs the right information, equipment and sequence. The next trade must be able to follow without undoing what has just been achieved.

These are construction management responsibilities. Calling the product innovative does not discharge them.

This is why design for manufacture and assembly has to influence the design while choices are still open. Bringing a supplier in after the building has been substantially designed and the packages divided up can leave them trying to recover opportunities that have already been lost.

Buy the outcome, then organise the work

Clients have an important part in this. If they want a different result, they need a procurement process that allows the people responsible for manufacture and assembly to shape the solution early enough to matter.

That requires discipline from suppliers too. Early involvement should produce useful commitments: what can be manufactured reliably, what must be fixed in the design, which tolerances matter and how the assembly will be inspected. The client needs something more substantial than enthusiasm.

The feasibility should compare the whole project under each realistic option. Include the design and coordination effort, factory and site work, transport and installation, temporary works, financing implications and remaining risks. Test whether a claimed saving in one activity changes the completion date. A faster installation will not bring occupation forward if another unresolved package still controls the programme.

Likewise, count the work wherever it occurs. A reduction in site labour is an important operational change; it is not, on its own, proof that the total labour needed to deliver the building has fallen. We should be able to explain both.

Clients also need to understand what happens if the plan is interrupted. Who holds the design information? How can unfinished work be completed? What evidence accompanies a concealed assembly? Who coordinates a remedy where a defect crosses the boundary between manufacture and installation?

Those questions should be resolved in the project’s arrangements. The customer should not have to discover the gaps after something goes wrong.

Give good suppliers a fair test

I do not want the demand for evidence to become another way of defending business as usual. New approaches need opportunities to demonstrate what they can do. Capable suppliers also need enough continuity to learn, invest and improve.

A repeat client can help by testing a clearly defined approach across a suitable group of projects. Agree the comparison in advance. Measure the complete process and record what needed to change. Be prepared to report a result that is less impressive than the original claim, as well as one that exceeds it.

That gives the next client something useful to build on. It also helps the supplier distinguish a repeatable capability from a successful one-off demonstration.

The opportunity extends beyond factories. Designers, constructors, financiers and clients all have to understand the enterprise and delivery model around the product. Otherwise a promising component can be trapped inside a process that was never organised to use it well.

I have argued for years that modern construction needs to be measurably better. Prefabrication can contribute to that. So can better planning of work that remains on site. The combination deserves more attention than a contest between labels.

Show the customer the completed proposition. Put the costs, the programme and the responsibilities alongside the claimed benefits. Then let the evidence build confidence.

That is how prefab earns its place in the feasibility.

]]><![CDATA[Build to order: a different starting point for smaller apartments]]>https://theconstructionedge.substack.com/p/build-to-order-a-different-startinghttps://theconstructionedge.substack.com/p/build-to-order-a-different-startingTue, 27 Oct 2026 00:05:07 GMTWhat changes if a smaller apartment project begins with a defined group of people who want the homes, rather than a product assembled first and sold to whoever the market later supplies?

That is the question behind my interest in build-to-order housing. It is not a claim that households can dispense with development expertise. It is a proposal to examine whether organising demand differently can produce a better fit between the homes, the delivery model and the people who will occupy them.

The attraction is understandable. The difficult work is establishing an arrangement that can be financed, governed and completed without asking households to carry risks they do not understand.

Subscribe now

Define what the group is buying

A group of interested buyers is not yet a viable project. The participants need a suitable site, a realistic product and a clear understanding of the total commitment. They also need professional capability to test the opportunity before enthusiasm becomes an obligation.

Their interests will not be identical. Households may have different budgets, timeframes, accessibility needs and preferences about common facilities. The project needs a way to resolve those differences without redesigning the building every time an individual changes their mind.

A defined family of layouts and options could help. The purpose would be to offer meaningful choice while retaining enough consistency to support design, pricing and construction. Customisation should be assessed for its effect on the whole project, including other participants.

The offer also needs clear boundaries. What is included? What remains provisional? Which costs sit outside the construction price? A household should not be attracted by a narrow figure that excludes the work needed to turn a site into an occupied home.

Put a competent delivery organisation around it

Someone must perform the development functions. Site assessment, approvals, design coordination, procurement, finance and project management do not disappear because the buyers are known earlier.

The arrangement should identify who performs each function, how decisions are made and what authority the participants retain. It should explain how advisers are appointed, how conflicts are handled and how the group receives independent information about progress and exposure.

There also needs to be a route through disagreement. What happens if a participant wants to withdraw, cannot meet a commitment or disputes a change? How are additional costs considered? What happens to the programme while a decision is made?

These are not peripheral details to be settled after the group forms. They are part of the product. The legal and financial structure needs competent design for the actual circumstances, with the household’s understanding treated as an objective rather than an obstacle.

A good delivery model should make participation more intelligible. If it requires every purchaser to become a sophisticated developer, it is unlikely to serve the households the proposal is intended to help.

Test where a saving could genuinely come from

There may be opportunities to reduce uncertainty about the customer, improve repeatability and organise the transaction differently. Those opportunities need to be tested against the complete cost and risk of delivery.

Land still has a cost, including where an existing owner contributes it. Professional work still needs to be done. Construction still needs a viable business behind it. The financing arrangement has costs and conditions. A different label does not remove any of those realities.

A claimed saving should therefore have an explanation. Which activity has been removed or improved? Which uncertainty has been reduced? Which cost has shifted to another participant? What allowance remains for things that do not proceed as expected?

Progress payments deserve particularly careful consideration if proposed. Earlier purchaser contributions may change the financing requirement, but they also change the household’s exposure during delivery. Any claim that the model offers completion certainty must be supported by a defined, credible arrangement. It cannot rest on the reassuring use of the word guarantee.

The relevant comparison is a completed home and a transparent account of the commitments required to obtain it. A lower initial funding estimate is not the same thing.

Give a practical model a fair trial

My recent housing writing has proposed a time-limited delivery agency to support a different route into smaller apartment projects. The point is to create a capable organisation with a clear task, including helping suitable project-home builders develop the additional capability the work requires. 1

That broader proposal needs detailed development. Build-to-order is one delivery question within it, not a set of terms that can be assumed from the name of the initiative.

I would start with a carefully selected project and a defined customer group. Test the site, product, governance and financing proposition before presenting it as ready for wider use. Establish what will be measured and make the assumptions available for scrutiny by the participants and their advisers.

The evaluation should follow the project through occupation. Did the homes suit the intended households? Were the final commitments understood from the outset? How did decisions and changes work? What was the total cost, and what capability could be carried into the next project?

Successful elements could then be repeated. Difficulties should be reported plainly, not concealed to protect the appeal of the model. Households should not become the unpaid test bed for an idea whose risks have not been worked through.

There is room to challenge the conventional starting point for smaller apartment development. The case will be stronger when the alternative can explain its responsibilities as clearly as its ambitions.

Build to order should mean organising a better proposition around the customer. It must not mean leaving the customer to organise the missing parts.

]]><![CDATA[Welcome to Construction Edge]]>https://theconstructionedge.substack.com/p/welcome-to-the-construction-edgehttps://theconstructionedge.substack.com/p/welcome-to-the-construction-edgeSat, 24 Oct 2026 01:42:12 GMTConstruction has no shortage of people telling us what is wrong. The harder work is deciding what to change, who will take responsibility, and how we will know whether it made a measurable and enduring difference.

That is what I want Construction Edge to be about.

I have spent much of my working life asking how we could build better. From my start as a building cadet, leading the construction of Australia’s New Parliament House, as Managing Director of large housing businesses in Australia and around the Pacific Rim, resolving distressed businesses and projects, as and academic and leader in the modern construction narrative and as NSW’s inaugural Building Commissioner all have sharpened the customer end of that question. A building is somebody’s home, workplace or long-term investment. Society has a right to expect the people who deliver today’s buildings to know what they are doing and stand behind the result.

Through Construction Edge, my independent advisory work brings those questions to clients, constructors and people shaping the industry. This publication gives me room to work through the arguments in public, beyond a brief comment or a presentation slide. I hope readers will feel comfortable to contribute constructively and respectfully.

Start with the customer

We often divide construction into separate conversations. Housing supply is discussed in one room. Productivity in another. Quality turns up when something has gone wrong. Skills, procurement, design and regulation each have their own participants and their own explanations. Then there is insurance and finance.

The customer gets the combined result.

A late design decision can become a procurement problem, then an installation problem, then a defect someone else has to fix. A cheap package can leave an expensive building to operate. A planning approval can promise housing that the available delivery model cannot make viable.

If we want a different result, we need to follow those connections far enough to find the decision that could change it. There is little value in asking the last person in the chain to solve a problem created much earlier.

That will be a recurring theme here: looking beyond each participant’s account of their own performance to what the whole project delivers.

What you can expect

I will write about construction cost and productivity, building quality, housing delivery and the enterprises and people needed to improve them. Some pieces will examine a particular practice. Others will test an idea or argue for a change in how clients, industry and government approach their responsibilities.

Modern construction methods will feature. So will the less fashionable work of getting design, procurement and assembly properly organised. A new material, factory or digital platform should be able to explain what it improves for a project and its customer. The announcement is the beginning of that conversation.

I am interested in smaller constructors as well as large organisations. Capability does not become useful only when it comes with a large balance sheet. We need to understand what allows a sound enterprise to develop, repeat good work, to improve margins and business value and remain accountable after handover.

There will also be arguments about the homes we offer, the neighbourhoods they create and the costs households carry after settlement. Counting dwellings matters. Understanding whether those dwellings meet people’s needs matters too.

Some readers will know my writing from LinkedIn or earlier Construction Edge articles. This is a place for the longer argument. I will return to earlier ideas where they remain useful, but they need to face today’s conditions. Having argued something for years does not relieve any of us of the need to test it again.

Expect a view

I will have opinions. Readers who know me will not find that surprising. I also want to distinguish what the evidence shows, what I think it means and what I am proposing should happen next. I want to contribute to good for one, good for all outcomes.

You should expect direct criticism of practices that leave customers, constructors and the public carrying avoidable cost or risk. You can also expect recognition of people doing useful work. There are capable clients, constructors, designers, manufacturers, lawyers, insurers, financiers and educators whose experience deserves a wider hearing.

Disagreement is welcome. If a proposal will not work, explain the constraint and offer a better way. If you have improved an outcome, show what changed, how you measured it and what someone else could learn. A claim becomes much more interesting when it can survive those questions.

My aim is for each essay to leave the reader with something specific to consider: a decision to revisit, a question to put to a project team, or a better test of a claim being made. Importantly, how we can all contribute to a valued construction industry.

Subscribe if that is a conversation you want to be part of. Bring the experience of your own work to it. The industry has enough problems worth solving without spending all our effort defending how we have always done things.

Let’s give more attention to what we are prepared to change.

Subscribe for free to receive new posts.
